setupSteps: Choose the dumbbells. FitPlate beginner start: about 2-4 kg each (est.), or lighter if you cannot hold a pause at the top without swinging. Sources give lifters 15-25 lb (about 7-11 kg) only as an experienced range; those are pound figures converted by me.
Stand with feet hip-width apart, knees soft, ribs down, abdominals braced, chest tall.
Hold one dumbbell in each hand at your sides, palms facing in, a very slight bend in the elbows (est. 10-20 degrees from straight, not a bicep curl).
Check the mirror or a camera in front, so you can see both arms and shoulders at the same height.
Set the pulley at its lowest position and clip on a single handle.
Stand side-on to the stack, about one arm's length away, feet hip-width apart.

Hold the handle with the hand on the side far from the stack, so the cable crosses in front of your thighs and the raise moves away from the stack. Sources differ (some say the near hand, one says outside hand); FitPlate chooses the far hand because the line of pull is cleaner and the cable does not rub your leg.
Optional: hold the stack or an upright with your other hand and lean away about 10-30 degrees (est.; one source gives 20-30 degrees) for a longer range; beginners should start upright.
Select a very small weight on the stack (the lightest plates, often about 2.5-5 kg per plate, est.; machine plate weights vary and are not standard). Pin the stack carefully.
Sit on an upright bench with feet flat on the floor, back tall, dumbbells at your sides. No source gave an exact bench angle; use a fully upright seat (about 90 degrees, est.).
Seated removes leg and hip momentum, so use a lighter weight than standing.

steps.title: Stand tall and brace
steps.action: Feet hip-width, ribs down, abdominals tight, shoulders down and back (not shrugged).
steps.visualCheck: Front: both shoulders level, arms straight down; side: ears over shoulders.

steps.title: Soften the elbows
steps.action: Keep a slight, fixed bend in each elbow and hold it for the whole rep.
steps.visualCheck: Front: small bend only, not a curl.

steps.title: Start the raise by moving the elbows out
steps.action: Lift the elbows out to the sides and slightly forward, as if pushing the dumbbells away from your body; the hands stay at about the same height as the elbows.
steps.feel: Burn in the side of the shoulder.
steps.visualCheck: Front: elbows rise first; hands are not higher than the elbows.

steps.title: Do not shrug
steps.action: Keep the shoulders pulled gently down away from the ears the whole way up.
steps.feel: Long neck, side shoulder doing the work, not the top of the neck.
steps.visualCheck: Front: shoulders stay level and low; no rise toward the ears.

steps.title: Lift to about shoulder height
steps.action: Stop when the upper arms are about level with the shoulders, in line with or slightly in front of your body line.
steps.feel: Tension peaks in the side shoulder.
steps.visualCheck: Front: elbows at about shoulder height, arms making a rough T or Y shape (arm angle to the trunk about 80-90 degrees, est.).

steps.title: Pause briefly
steps.breathing: Hold the breath only for a moment; do not strain.
steps.visualCheck: Front: no sway; side: trunk still.

steps.title: Lower slowly
steps.action: Lower the dumbbells in a smooth arc back to the sides.
steps.feel: Side shoulder controlling the weight down.
steps.visualCheck: Front: arms come back symmetrically; no drop or swing.

steps.title: Reset and repeat
steps.action: Pause briefly at the bottom (do not rest the weights on your thighs), then start the next rep.

commonMistakes.title: Using too heavy a weight
commonMistakes.text: Using too heavy a weight. Why: form breaks, momentum takes over and the neck muscles do the work. Fix: drop the weight until you can hold a 1-second pause at the top with no swinging; most sources suggest going lighter than you think.

commonMistakes.title: Swinging the body to start the lift
commonMistakes.text: Swinging the body to start the lift. Why: it takes the work off the side shoulder and adds back strain. Fix: stand tall, brace, and keep the hips still (or use the seated version).

commonMistakes.title: Shrugging the shoulders
commonMistakes.text: Shrugging the shoulders. Why: the upper trapezius takes over from the side shoulder. Fix: keep the shoulders down and think of pushing the dumbbells away from you rather than lifting them up.

commonMistakes.title: Lifting above shoulder height
commonMistakes.text: Lifting above shoulder height. Why: the upper trapezius takes over and a 2013 survey of 77 male lifters linked raises above 90 degrees with impingement characteristics (correlation only). Fix: stop when the upper arms reach shoulder height.

commonMistakes.title: Leading with the hands, with the wrists higher than the elbows
commonMistakes.text: Leading with the hands, with the wrists higher than the elbows. Why: it shifts load to the shoulder front and makes the lift feel like pouring a jug. Fix: lead with the elbows and keep the hands level with or below the elbows (ExRx wording).

commonMistakes.title: Locking the elbows straight or bending them too much
commonMistakes.text: Locking the elbows straight or bending them too much. Why: straight elbows load the elbow joint, deep bends turn it into a curl-and-press. Fix: keep a small, fixed bend (est. 10-20 degrees from straight).

commonMistakes.title: Dropping the weights quickly
commonMistakes.text: Dropping the weights quickly. Why: you lose half the work and may jolt the shoulder. Fix: lower in 2-3 seconds.

commonMistakes.title: Letting the cable snap back at the bottom
commonMistakes.text: Letting the cable snap back at the bottom. Why: the stack slams and the handle yanks the arm. Fix: control the return and do not rest at the bottom.

commonMistakes.title: Raising straight out to the side with thumbs pointing down
commonMistakes.text: Raising straight out to the side with thumbs pointing down. Why: the "pouring the jug" position internally rotates the shoulder and sources link it to a narrower subacromial space (ACE noted slight external rotation after 60-70 degrees may reduce impingement risk; coach-level, not proven). Fix: keep the palm facing down or neutral and the elbow slightly in front of the shoulder line.

safetyNotes: Keep the load light. The lateral raise has a long lever arm, so a few kilograms is enough. If you need a swing to lift it, the weight is too heavy.

Shoulder impingement: the evidence is mixed. Kolber et al. (2013, 77 male lifters, correlational) found lateral raises above 90 degrees were associated with clinical signs of impingement, and suggested avoiding raises beyond 90 degrees and strengthening the external rotators. A sports medicine writer argues the risk reasons above shoulder height are weakly supported; ACE's page says slight external rotation at 60-70 degrees may reduce impingement risk. Practical advice: stop at about shoulder height, keep the elbow slightly in front, keep the shoulders down, lighten the load, and stop with sharp or pinching pain. ExRx also warns that shoulder blade protraction can narrow the subacromial space (on the related front raise page).
High blood pressure: avoid long breath-holding; stop 2-3 reps before failure.
Cable station: check the pin and handle, do not walk away with the stack raised; return the handle gently.
Gym etiquette: re-rack dumbbells in the correct place, wipe the handle, do not film other members, do not hog the cable station during long rests.

Note: all sources for this item were seen only as search-result summaries (pages not opened in full); many are fitness-site and coaching blogs. The abduction thresholds (25 and 75 and 100 degrees), the swing limit (10 degrees), the shrug threshold (15 percent), the 2 s minimum rep, the starting weights, the stack-plate sizes and all sets, reps and rest values are FitPlate choices (est.), not validated. Not found: a full ACE, NASM, NSCA, Harvard Health, NHS or Mayo Clinic page with lateral raise steps; ExRx muscle lists; a lateral-raise-specific professional-body prescription; a lateral-raise-specific Compendium code; a peer-reviewed standard for starting load or stopping angle; a validated seated bench angle; direct evidence that lateral raises cause impingement (Kolber 2013 is correlational); condition-specific sources for knee pain, lower back pain, obesity and PCOS; the primary ACOG page.

conditionCautions.change: No long breath-holding; stop 2-3 reps before failure; no lifting if resting BP >= 180/120; uncontrolled BP: ask a doctor

conditionCautions.change: 2-3 non-consecutive resistance days per week; usual glucose checks if on insulin or sulfonylureas
conditionCautions.source: ADA position statement, Colberg et al. 2016

conditionCautions.change: After clearance: light loads, continuous breathing, no straining; arm work above the heart can raise blood pressure more
